lesson.title: Units on the Derivative: Making dy/dx Mean Something
lesson.summary: A derivative always carries units, the units of the output divided by the units of the input, and reading those units correctly is what turns a bare number into a meaningful rate.
lesson.body:
Every derivative comes with units attached, and the rule for finding them is simple: the units of dy/dx are the units of y divided by the units of x. This follows directly from how the derivative was built out of instantaneous rate: it is the limit of Delta y over Delta x, and Delta y over Delta x plainly carries units of y over units of x at every step along the way. Taking a limit changes the number's precision, not the units riding along with it, so the derivative inherits exactly the same units as the difference quotient it came from.

A physical example makes this concrete. If s(t) measures position in meters and t measures time in seconds, then s'(t) = ds/dt carries units of meters per second, which is precisely what everyday language calls speed. Consider free-fall distance, s(t) = 4.9t^2 meters after t seconds of falling. Then s'(t) = 9.8t, and at t = 3 seconds, s'(3) = 9.8(3) = 29.4 meters per second: the object is falling at a rate of 29.4 meters per second at that exact instant, a statement that only makes sense once the units meters per second are attached to the number 29.4.

The same rule explains why the marginal quantities from the last several chapters read so naturally as prices and rates. Marginal cost C'(x) in an earlier chapter came out to $70 per unit at x = 50, because cost is measured in dollars and x counts items, so dC/dx automatically carries units of dollars per unit, exactly the units of a price tag. Marginal revenue and marginal profit carry the same dollars-per-unit units for the identical reason: y is dollars, x is a count of items, and dy/dx is dollars divided by units.

Checking units is also one of the fastest sanity checks available on a derivative. If a velocity calculation comes out in meters instead of meters per second, something was set up wrong before any arithmetic mistake even gets a chance to hide. In an applied problem, a derivative's numeric value should always travel with its units: $7 per unit, 29.4 meters per second, never just 7 or 29.4 sitting alone.
